t: #2479 Maximum XOR of Two Non-Overlapping Subtrees
o: First compute each node's subtree sum via DFS. Two subtrees are non-overlapping iff neither node is an ancestor of the other. Key observation: when standing at node u during a DFS, the valid partners for subtree(u) are exactly the subtree sums already inserted into a global binary trie — namely subtrees hanging off the current root-to-u path to the left. So we insert each child's entire subtree-sum collection into the trie right before recursing into it, and query the trie with the child's subtree sum before insertion. Example 1: subtree sums are [26,16,8,6,2,5]; 16⊕8=24. Example 2 (chain): no disjoint pair ever meets in the trie, so the answer stays 0.
k: Subtree sums via one post-order pass; XOR maximization via a binary trie over 64-bit sums.
Insert a child's whole subtree-sum list (small-to-large merged) into the trie just before descending into it — guarantees only disjoint subtrees are ever compared.
Query before insert ensures each disjoint pair is considered exactly once.

a.n: Approach 1: DFS + binary trie with small-to-large lists
a.i: Build rooted tree, compute subtree sums and per-node lists of all sums in the subtree (merged small-to-large, O(n log n) total). DFS: for each child c, query trie with sum(c), then insert all of c's list, then recurse.
s: Root at 0 via BFS; process nodes in reverse BFS order to compute subtree sums and merged lists.
Implement a binary trie (children pointers + counts) over ~46-bit sums.
DFS: for each child c — ans = max(ans, trie.query(sum[c])); insert every value in list[c]; recurse into c.
a.t: O(n log n · B) — small-to-large merging touches each sum O(log n) times, each trie op is O(B=46).
a.sp: O(n log n) for the merged lists plus O(n·B) for the trie.

w: This is the intended hard-tier solution. Pitfalls: comparing overlapping subtrees (ancestors/descendants must never meet in the trie — the insert-before-descend discipline handles it), bit width (sums reach 5·10¹³, so 46 bits), and recursion depth on chains (iterative BFS ordering helps). Follow-up: maximize XOR of two disjoint paths, or handle vertex updates.
